title: Feelings & opinions
verifiedBy: Fable (Claude Fable 5) — LLM review, authorised by repo owner

rules.text: The pair that carries the module: li-ʾanna introduces the REASON and li-dhālika introduces the CONSEQUENCE. The same two facts go either way round — lā urīd al-qahwa li-ʾannī taʿbān, or anā taʿbān, li-dhālika lā urīd al-qahwa.

li-ʾanna cannot sit straight in front of a verb the way English "because" can. It needs a noun or an attached pronoun: li-ʾannī (because I), li-ʾannaka (because you-m), li-ʾannaki (you-f), li-ʾannahu (because he), li-ʾanna al-qahwa bārida (because the coffee is cold).

li- is a clitic meaning "for, to", glued to the front of what follows it: li-ʾanna is "for that", li-dhālika is "for that reason". limādhā ("why") comes from the same li- but is written solid, as one word, and never splits.

When the reason is a NOUN rather than a whole sentence, Arabic switches to bi-sabab ("by reason of"): bi-sabab al-jaww, because of the weather. English splits the same way — "because" against "because of" — so the trap is putting a bare noun after li-ʾanna.

Feelings ride M1's verbless sentence and there is no "am" or "is" to place: anā taʿbān, anā jāʾiʿ, al-ʿamal muhimm. English cannot say any of these without a verb, and that missing verb is what a learner keeps trying to supply.

The adjective agrees with the SUBJECT of its sentence — whoever the sentence is about, not whoever is speaking. anā taʿbān from a man, anā taʿbāna from a woman; and hal anti ḥazīna? is asked OF a woman, whoever is doing the asking.
limādhā asks why and stands at the front, needing no hal beside it; the answer comes back with li-ʾanna. limādhā anta ḥazīn? — li-ʾannī taʿbān.
fī raʾyī ("in my opinion") is the softener an opinion wants, and it is a phrase and not a verb: the sentence behind it is the same verbless one — fī raʾyī, al-ʿarabiyya ṣaʿba.

Bounded on purpose: negate a verb with M3's lā and leave the verbless sentences affirmative. laysa is what a verbless sentence would need and L1 never teaches it, so no reason clause here may reach for it.

jāʾiʿ carries both of Arabic's throat letters in one short word: the ʾ in its middle is hamza and the ʿ at its end is ʿayn. They are different consonants and this course never lets them collapse into one another — write ʾ for the first and ʿ for the second.

sentences.display: anā taʿbān li-ʾannī dhahabtu ilā al-ʿamal
sentences.script: أنا تعبان لأني ذهبت إلى العمل
sentences.cue: I am tired because I went to work (said by a man)
sentences.literal: I tired because-I went-I to the-work

words.note: "Because" — never bare before a verb; it carries the person with the suffixes of ismī: li-ʾannī (because I), li-ʾannaka, li-ʾannaki, li-ʾannahu. Before a noun it stays plain: li-ʾanna al-qahwa.

sentences.trap: English "because I went" puts the pronoun in the second half; Arabic puts it on the back of the because-word itself, and the verb after it keeps its own person too.
sentences.sound: a-NAA taʿ-BAAN li-ʾan-NEE dha-HAB-tu i-LAA al-ʿA-mal — the n of li-ʾannī is held doubled.

variations.display: anā taʿbāna li-ʾannī dhahabtu ilā al-ʿamal
variations.script: أنا تعبانة لأني ذهبت إلى العمل
variations.cue: I am tired because I went to work (said by a woman)
variations.changed: add -a to the adjective — the because-word does not change at all

variations.display: anā taʿbān li-ʾannahu dhahaba ilā al-ʿamal
variations.script: أنا تعبان لأنه ذهب إلى العمل
variations.cue: I am tired because he went to work
variations.changed: -ī → -ahu, and the verb follows it to he

variations.cue: Why are you tired? (to a man)
variations.changed: the question the sentence answers — limādhā, and li-ʾannī will carry the reply

mistake.display: anā taʿbān li-ʾanna dhahabtu ilā al-ʿamal
mistake.script: أنا تعبان لأن ذهبت إلى العمل
mistake.why: The English shape: "because" then straight into the verb. li-ʾanna needs a noun or a pronoun welded to it first — li-ʾannī dhahabtu.

sentences.usage: The most ordinary explanation there is, and the sentence this whole module is built to make.
sentences.mnemonic: li-ʾann-ī — "for-that-I": the because carries the who.

sentences.cue: I am hungry, so I'll eat the bread (said by a man)

words.note: "Hungry" — jāʾiʿ of a man, jāʾiʿa of a woman. Two throat letters in one short word, not the same one: the ʾ in the middle is hamza, a catch in the breath; the ʿ at the end is ʿayn, deeper down.
"For that" — the consequence word, where li-ʾanna is the reason word. dhālika is "that", the far-pointing partner of M8's hādhā, with li- glued on. It opens the second half, where English puts "so".

sentences.trap: li-ʾanna and li-dhālika point opposite ways. Reason first then li-dhālika; consequence first then li-ʾanna. Getting them the wrong way round reverses the sentence.
sentences.sound: a-NAA JAA-ʾiʿ, li-DHAA-li-ka SAA-kul al-KHUBZ — the ʿ at the end of jāʾiʿ closes the word off in the throat.

variations.cue: I'll eat the bread because I am hungry
variations.changed: the same two facts, reversed — and the joining word flips with them

variations.cue: I am hungry, so I'll eat the bread (said by a woman)
variations.changed: add -a: the adjective follows the person it describes

variations.display: anā jāʾiʿ li-ʾannī lā ākul fī aṣ-ṣabāḥ
variations.script: أنا جائع لأني لا آكل في الصباح
variations.cue: I am hungry because I don't eat in the morning (said by a man)
variations.changed: a negated habit as the reason: lā rides inside the li-ʾannī clause

mistake.why: This says the hunger is caused by the eating. li-ʾanna gives a reason; the consequence word is li-dhālika: anā jāʾiʿ, li-dhālika sa-ākul.

sentences.usage: Announcing what you are about to do, and why you have to.
sentences.mnemonic: li-dhālika — "for that": that is why, so here is what happens next.

sentences.cue: Why are you sad? (to a man)

words.note: "Why" — literally "for what", written solid as one word: it never splits into li- and the rest the way li-ʾanna and li-dhālika do. Like ayna and matā it stands at the front and needs no hal.
"Sad" — ḥazīn of a man, ḥazīna of a woman, agreeing with the SUBJECT of its sentence like every adjective since ṭālib. It opens with the breathy ḥ, not the plain h of hal.

sentences.trap: The adjective follows whoever the question is ABOUT. Asked of a woman it is ḥazīna, no matter who is asking.
sentences.sound: li-MAA-dhā AN-ta ḥa-ZEEN — limādhā holds its long ā in the middle.

variations.cue: Why are you sad? (to a woman)
variations.changed: anti and ḥazīna: the question turns to a woman and the adjective follows her

variations.cue: Why are you angry? (to a man)
variations.changed: swap the feeling — the frame is the frame

variations.cue: I am sad because the weather is cold (said by a man)
variations.changed: the answer the question fishes for: li-ʾanna, and a whole reason behind it

mistake.why: Two question markers on one question. hal turns a statement into a yes/no question; limādhā already asks. One or the other, as with ayna in M7.

sentences.usage: The question that opens every conversation about how someone is doing.
sentences.mnemonic: limādhā — "for what?": the why that is spelled as one piece.

sentences.cue: I am angry because the coffee is cold (said by a man)

words.note: "Angry" — ghāḍib of a man, ghāḍiba of a woman. It opens with the gargled gh of ghadan and carries the heavy ḍ in its middle, the same one as in min faḍlika.

sentences.trap: In front of a NOUN, li-ʾanna stays plain — no suffix. It is only in front of a verb that it must borrow a pronoun.

variations.cue: I am angry because the coffee is cold (said by a woman)
variations.changed: add -a: the adjective follows the person it describes

variations.cue: I am angry because the car is expensive
variations.changed: a different reason, and the second half is still a whole verbless sentence

variations.cue: The coffee is cold, so I am angry (said by a man)
variations.changed: the same two facts turned round — reason first, and li-dhālika hands over the anger

mistake.why: A pronoun AND a noun, both doing the same job. li-ʾanna takes one or the other: li-ʾanna al-qahwa bārida, or li-ʾannahā bārida.

sentences.usage: Complaining precisely — the feeling, then the thing that caused it.
sentences.mnemonic: ghāḍib — the gh growls, which is what anger does.

words.note: "Lovely, beautiful" — jamīl of a masculine thing, jamīla of a feminine one. mūsīqā is feminine, so the -a here. The everyday word of approval for anything from music to weather.

sentences.trap: The adjective agrees with the THING, not with the person admiring it. mūsīqā is feminine, so jamīla — whoever is speaking.
sentences.sound: al-moo-SEE-qā ja-MEE-la JID-dan — jiddan holds its doubled d, as it has since M3.

variations.cue: The book is very lovely
variations.changed: a masculine thing, so the adjective goes bare

variations.cue: In my opinion, the music is lovely
variations.changed: the same judgement, offered as an opinion rather than a fact

variations.cue: Is the music lovely?
variations.changed: the judgement asked instead of stated — hal, and still no verb anywhere

mistake.why: mūsīqā is a feminine noun despite its ending, so its adjective takes -a: jamīla. Gender belongs to the noun and is learned with it — M3's law, still running.

sentences.usage: Saying you like something, without saying "I like".
sentences.mnemonic: jamīl — the root of "Jamila", the name that means beautiful.

sentences.cue: In my opinion, Arabic is difficult

words.note: M7's fī plus raʾy ("opinion") wearing M1's -ī: "in my opinion", learned whole. The hamza in raʾyī is written — raʾy, not *rāy — and the sentence after it stays verbless.
The Arabic language, a feminine noun — so its adjectives take -a: al-ʿarabiyya ṣaʿba, al-ʿarabiyya jamīla. It opens with ʿayn, not hamza. The article is kept: Arabic names its language "the Arabic".
"Difficult" — ṣaʿb of a masculine thing, ṣaʿba of a feminine one. Heavy ṣ at the front and ʿayn in the middle; its opposite, sahl, turns up in the next sentence.

sentences.trap: fī raʾyī is not a verb and adds none. The sentence after the comma is the same verbless statement it would have been on its own.
sentences.sound: fee RAʾ-yee, al-ʿa-ra-BEE-ya ṢAʿ-ba — the catch in raʾyī is audible between the two syllables.

variations.cue: In my opinion, Arabic is beautiful
variations.changed: the other opinion, in the same frame

variations.cue: Arabic is difficult because the books are big
variations.changed: attach a reason with li-ʾanna and a noun

variations.display: fī raʾyī, al-ʿarabiyya jamīla wa ṣaʿba
variations.cue: In my opinion, Arabic is beautiful and difficult
variations.changed: wa lets one opinion hold two adjectives — both agree with al-ʿarabiyya

mistake.why: al-ʿarabiyya is feminine, so the adjective takes -a: ṣaʿba. The language names itself with a feminine ending and its adjectives have to follow.

sentences.usage: Softening a judgement so it stays a conversation.
sentences.mnemonic: fī raʾyī — "in my view": the Arabic hedge, one phrase long.

sentences.cue: This is easy, so I am happy (said by a man)

words.note: "Easy" — sahl of a masculine thing, sahla of a feminine one, and the plain opposite of ṣaʿb. The h in the middle is the light one, the same as in hal.

sentences.trap: Two whole sentences, joined. Each half stands on its own with no verb in it, and li-dhālika is the hinge between them.

variations.cue: Arabic is easy, so I am happy
variations.changed: name the thing, and the adjective takes -a to match it

variations.cue: I am happy because this is easy
variations.changed: the same two facts, reversed, with li-ʾanna instead

variations.cue: This is hard, so I am sad (said by a man)
variations.changed: the whole line in negative: ṣaʿb brings ḥazīn with it, and li-dhālika still hinges

mistake.why: Said by a man this is wrong: -a describes a female subject. He says anā saʿīd — the adjective follows the person the sentence is about, which here is the speaker.

sentences.usage: The relieved half of any conversation about learning.
sentences.mnemonic: sahl — a plain, flat, easy thing; sahl is also a plain in the ground.

sentences.display: lā adhhab ilā as-sūq bi-sabab al-jaww
sentences.script: لا أذهب إلى السوق بسبب الجو
sentences.cue: I am not going to the market because of the weather
sentences.literal: not go-I to the-market by-reason-of the-weather

words.note: "By reason of" — M2's bi- glued to sabab ("reason"). This is the because that takes a NOUN: bi-sabab al-jaww, bi-sabab al-ʿamal. li-ʾanna takes a whole sentence instead, and the two never swap jobs.

sentences.trap: "Because" splits in two here exactly as it does in English: because + sentence is li-ʾanna, because of + noun is bi-sabab. Putting a bare noun after li-ʾanna is the error.
sentences.sound: LAA ADH-hab i-LAA as-SOOQ bi-SA-bab al-JAWW.

variations.display: lā adhhab ilā as-sūq li-ʾanna al-jaww bārid
variations.script: لا أذهب إلى السوق لأن الجو بارد
variations.cue: I am not going to the market because the weather is cold
variations.changed: the same reason as a whole sentence, so the word changes to li-ʾanna

variations.display: lā adhhab ilā al-ʿamal bi-sabab al-jaww
variations.script: لا أذهب إلى العمل بسبب الجو
variations.cue: I am not going to work because of the weather
variations.changed: swap the destination — the reason phrase holds

variations.cue: I will be at home because of the weather
variations.changed: bi-sabab serves any tense: the sa- future stays home for the same noun reason

mistake.display: lā adhhab ilā as-sūq li-ʾanna al-jaww
mistake.script: لا أذهب إلى السوق لأن الجو
mistake.why: li-ʾanna needs a whole sentence after it and "the weather" is only half of one. Either finish it — li-ʾanna al-jaww bārid — or switch to the noun-taking form: bi-sabab al-jaww.

sentences.usage: Excusing yourself from something, with the cause named and nothing more said.
sentences.mnemonic: bi-sabab — "by the cause of"; sabab is the reason itself.

sentences.cue: Work is important because I want a car

words.note: "Important" — muhimm of a masculine thing, muhimma of a feminine one. The m at its end is held doubled, which is what the second m in the spelling is for.

sentences.trap: The first half is a verbless sentence about a thing, the second is a verb sentence about a person, and li-ʾannī is what lets them share a breath.
sentences.sound: al-ʿA-mal mu-HIMM li-ʾan-NEE u-REED say-YAA-ra — muhimm ends on a held m.

variations.cue: Work is important because he wants a car
variations.changed: -ī → -ahu, and the verb follows it to he

variations.cue: School is important because I am a student
variations.changed: a feminine subject takes -a, and the reason is verbless too

variations.cue: Why is work important?
variations.changed: limādhā over a thing: why is it — the verbless question the sentence answers

mistake.why: ʿamal is masculine, so the adjective stays bare: al-ʿamal muhimm. The -a belongs with feminine subjects — al-madrasa muhimma.

sentences.usage: Explaining a choice — what matters, and what it is for.
sentences.mnemonic: muhimm — what matters; hamm is the concern it comes from.

sentences.cue: I don't want the coffee because I am going to sleep

words.note: M6's sa- on the verb "sleep": anām (I sleep) becomes sa-anām, the person still the prefix underneath — sa-tanām (you-m or she), sa-yanām (he). A reason can sit in any tense the course has taught.

sentences.trap: The negation is M3's lā and it stays on the VERB. The reason half has no negation at all — this level never negates a verbless sentence.

variations.cue: I am going to sleep, so I don't want the coffee
variations.changed: the same two facts turned round — reason first, consequence after li-dhālika

variations.cue: I don't want the coffee because I am tired (said by a man)
variations.changed: a verbless reason instead of a verb one — and it stays affirmative

variations.cue: He doesn't want the coffee because he is going to sleep
variations.changed: the whole line in the third person: yu-, li-ʾannahu, sa-yanām — three agreements, one him

mistake.why: lā goes in FRONT of the verb it negates, never after it: lā urīd. That has been the rule since M3, and a reason clause does not change it.

sentences.usage: Turning something down without giving offence — the reason does the work.
sentences.mnemonic: sa-anām — the sleep is tomorrow's, so the sa- goes first.
